Reverse transcriptase. An unusual polymerase that synthesizes DNA from an RNA template—the reverse of normal transcription. It originated in retroviruses and is now exploited extensively in molecular biology research and biotechnology. The enzyme converts single-stranded RNA into complementary DNA, which can be further amplified or integrated into genomes. Reverse transcriptase catalyzes the synthesis of DNA in the five-prime to three-prime direction using RNA in the three-prime to five-prime direction as its template. Its substrates are deoxyribonucleotide triphosphates, and notably, no primer is required for initiation. The enzyme derives from retroviral enzymes, with HIV reverse transcriptase being the most well-characterized. Its fidelity is lower than DNA polymerase but higher than RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. Common uses include cDNA synthesis for molecular cloning, gene expression analysis through RT-PCR, and first-strand synthesis for creating gene libraries. RT-PCR, which stands for reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction, involves reverse transcription followed by PCR amplification to detect and quantify RNA levels in samples. A key structural feature is the lack of three-prime to five-prime exonuclease activity, meaning the enzyme has no proofreading ability. It does possess an RNase H domain that degrades the RNA template after synthesis. Reverse transcriptase breaks the central dogma's unidirectional flow. Information normally travels DNA to RNA to protein, but this enzyme allows RNA to generate DNA. Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to convert their RNA genomes into DNA for integration into host chromatin, ensuring their persistence and replication. The enzyme's discovery was revolutionary for molecular biology, enabling researchers to capture expressed genes as cDNA libraries, bypassing introns and identifying what genes cells actually transcribe.
